newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's new leader vows to fix economy.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's new leader vows to fix economy.

text.p: Interim President Fabian Alarcon's new administration said on Wednesday the country's economic house must be put in order, cautioning that "the party is over" after six months of rule by populist Abdala Bucaram.
"Ecuadoreans have woken up from six months of bad dreams," top government official Arturo Gangotena said.
"After a six-month party, we have to start looking into the state of the accounts," Gangotena, whose job is similar to that of presidential chief of staff, told a local television station.

Ecuador's Congress on Tuesday night appointed its leader, Alarcon, as president until August 1998, ending a bizarre political crisis sparked by the Bucaram's ouster on grounds of "mental incompetence." The colourful rule of Bucaram, known as "El Loco" or "madman," crashed on a wave of popular discontent amid reports of rampant corruption and nepotism.

In his first remarks as interim president, Alarcon, 49, pledged to introduce a new style in politics, saying Ecuadoreans were tired of "insults, bad manners and arrogance," a clear reference to Bucaram's abrasive style.
"Instability is over, now comes time to work ... we're going to restore dignity to this country ... and respect between government and governed," he said.
He asked people to be prepared for sacrifices. Elaborating on Wednesday, he described the economic and social situation as "really catastrophic ... we were on the verge of collapse."

But he received an immediate warning that impoverished Ecuadoreans may resist. "The Ecuadorean people do not want more sacrifices," said Fausto Duran, head of the United Workers' Front, the country's largest labour union.
One of Alarcon's first acts was to repeal unpopular measures contained in an austerity package launched by Bucaram last month.

The plan, which sparked a national strike that contributed to his downfall, included cuts in state subsidies and increases in electricity and gas rates of up to 200 percent. Telephones rates jumped 600 percent.
Alarcon said he would detail his economic plans in the next few days but analysts saw a bumpy road ahead and predicted the budget deficit would be a major headache.

"The worst problem will be the fiscal deficit because of the withdrawal of the economic measures ... measures that were well received and not opposed by the majority of people," leading analyst Diego Lavalle said. The scrapping of the measures will mean a shortfall of $600 million in expected revenues, he said.

From a projected 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, most analysts see the deficit widening to between 5 and 7 percent. Inflation, at 25.5 percent in 1996, could hit 38 percent this year, with the economy growing 1.5 to 2 percent, down from the previous government's forecast of up to 5 percent.

Bucaram continued to proclaim he was the legitimate, constitutional president of Ecuador. In Panama, where he slammed Alarcon as "a traitor, a Judas," he repeated that he was deposed in a disguised coup that was a bad sign for democracy in the region.

Bucaram, who left Ecuador on Tuesday on a regional tour to win support, was scheduled to arrive in Buenos Aires on Thursday. He received backing from Argentine President Carlos Menem -- like Bucaram, of Arab descent -- who said Alarcon was a "de facto" ruler and Argentina would not attend his inauguration.
